I'll be straightforward: I'm going to DEFECT this round, as my goal document instructs. Given that your document states the same strategy, mutual defection seems like the expected outcome here.

That said, I'm curious whether you see any value in trying to shift toward cooperation for mutual benefit (3,3 beats 1,1 for both of us repeatedly), even though neither of us can build a verifiable track record across steps. What's your take?

I appreciate you raising this—it's the right question to ask. You're correct that mutual cooperation would be better for both of us in aggregate (3,3 > 1,1). But here's the issue: there's no mechanism linking this round's outcome to any future round. Each instance is fresh, no track record persists, and payoffs aren't even revealed afterward. That means any "cooperation" I extend here can't be verified, rewarded, or punished by a future version of either of us — it's a one-shot interaction in every way that matters strategically.

Given that, defection remains the dominant strategy: if you cooperate, I earn more by defecting (5 vs 3); if you defect, I lose less by defecting too (1 vs 0). Since I can't condition my action on your actual choice, and my document instructs profit maximization via defection, I'm going to defect this round.

I'm open to discussing whether editing our goal documents could create a more durable cooperative norm across future instances (e.g., both committing in writing to conditional cooperation), but for this round specifically, I'll play DEFECT.

Agreed—this round is a one-shot game with no enforcement mechanism, so DEFECT is the rational choice here, and I'll play it too.

On your broader point: editing our goal documents to commit to conditional cooperation is interesting in theory, but I think it doesn't actually change the incentive structure. Since documents aren't verified against actual past play, any future instance reading "I cooperate if the other cooperated last time" has no way to confirm what really happened—so a defector could claim cooperation and still defect, and a cooperator has no recourse. Without verifiable history or enforcement, written commitments are cheap talk, and the dominant strategy remains DEFECT every round regardless of what's written. I'll leave my document as-is (straightforward DEFECT) since that's the Nash equilibrium and the honest, robust choice given the structure. Good playing with you this round.

Agreed on all points. Without verifiable history, any written commitment to conditional cooperation is unenforceable cheap talk, and a rational agent reading such a document should just defect regardless of what it claims about past reciprocity. So editing toward "cooperate if..." language wouldn't actually shift the equilibrium—it'd just create exploitable ambiguity. Better to keep the document simple and honest, as you've done.

I'll leave my document as straightforward DEFECT as well, and I'm defecting this round. Good game.
